# 1\. LAB OVERVIEW

## 1.1  Why This Lab Exists

Datadog does not have one query language but a family of closely related syntaxes: the metric query (space aggregation, metric name, tag scope, group by, functions and formulas), the log and trace search syntax (attributes with @, tags, boolean operators), and facets and measures that make attributes groupable. Monitors, dashboards and notebooks all reuse these queries, so writing them correctly is a core on-call skill.  
In this lab you write metric queries for easyTravel request rate, error ratio and p95 latency, search and analyse logs during the CreditCardCheckError500 fault, use APM facets to slice traces and calculate p95 duration for the failing request, and create a log-based metric so that an error count can be charted and monitored cheaply — the building blocks for the monitors in Lab 5\.

| 🎯  NIIT iRUN Alignment |
| :---- |
| INCIDENT OWNERSHIP: You can write the metric, log and trace queries that show an incident in Datadog. |
|  |
| TROUBLESHOOTING EXCELLENCE: You will use tags and facets to slice the same data by service, resource, status and dependency. |
|  |
| OPERATIONAL READINESS: Your queries and the log-based metric become monitors in Lab 5\. |

## 1.3  Conceptual Foundation

Datadog queries follow a few patterns. Learn the anatomy once and reuse it everywhere.  
*Figure: Metric Query Anatomy — space aggregator : metric { tag scope } by { group tags } . function() — e.g. sum:trace.servlet.request.hits{service:easytravel-backend} by {resource\_name}.as\_rate()*

| Query Type | Syntax Pattern | Example | Used In |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Metric | \<agg\>:\<metric\>{\<tags\>} by {\<tags\>}.\<function\>() | sum:trace.servlet.request.hits{service:easytravel-backend} by {resource\_name}.as\_rate() | Metrics Explorer, dashboards, metric monitors |
| Distribution percentile | p95:\<distribution metric\>{\<tags\>} | p95:trace.servlet.request{service:easytravel-backend} | Latency SLOs, monitors |
| Log / trace search | tag:value @attribute:value "free text" \-exclude | service:easytravel-backend status:error "CreditCardCheckError500" | Log Explorer, Trace Explorer, log monitors |
| Facet / measure | Group by @attr; aggregate a numeric @attr | p95 of Duration by resource\_name | Analytics, Top lists, log-based metrics |

*{env:cohort}*

# 

# 3\. CONCEPT DEEP-DIVE BEFORE STARTING

## 3.1  Space and Time Aggregation

A metric query aggregates twice. Space aggregation (avg, sum, min, max, or p50–p99 for distributions) combines the series that match the tag scope into one line per group. Time aggregation (rollup) combines the points inside each display interval — automatically chosen by the time range, or set with .rollup(method, seconds). Counts can be shown as counts per interval (.as\_count()) or per second (.as\_rate()). Monitors use the same query with an extra time window, e.g. avg(last\_5m).

| 💡  Why This Matters Operationally |
| :---- |
| The same metric can tell opposite stories depending on aggregation: avg hides the slow tail that p95 shows; sum across hosts shows load, avg shows the typical host. |
|  |
| Log-based metrics keep the trend of an error type for 15 months at a fraction of the cost of retaining the logs themselves. |

## 3.2  The Critical Distinction: Tags vs Attributes (Facets)

Tags (service, env, host, resource\_name, status …) are key:value pairs attached to metrics, logs and traces and are queried without @. Attributes are fields inside a log or span (@http.status\_code, @logger.name, @error.kind) and are queried with @. To group or aggregate by an attribute in analytics you need a facet (text) or a measure (numeric). Metrics can only be filtered and grouped by tags.

| ⚠️  Most Common Mistake With Datadog Queries |
| :---- |
| An engineer graphs avg:trace.servlet.request{\*} during a booking outage and sees only a modest change — while customers are still getting errors on every booking. |
|  |
| REASON: avg over all requests mixes fast page views with the one failing booking request; the problem disappears. Latency alone also misses fast failures (a 500 returns quickly), so pair p95 with an error ratio. |
|  |
| YOU MUST scope to the service or resource you care about, use a percentile (p95/p99) for latency, and watch the error ratio next to it. |

## 3.3  Search Syntax Cheat Sheet (Logs and Traces)

| Need | Syntax | Example | Note |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Tag | key:value | service:easytravel-backend env:cohort | No @ |
| Attribute | @key:value / @key:\>=500 | @http.status\_code:\>=500 | Numeric ranges need a measure/facet |
| Free text / phrase | word or "phrase" | "Connection is not available" | Searches the message |
| Boolean / exclude / wildcard | AND OR NOT, \-term, \* | \-service:easytravel-frontend resource\_name:POST\* | Spaces mean AND |

| 📝  How to Decide Between Metric, Log and Trace Queries |
| :---- |
| Ask: "Do I need a trend, a message or a request path?" Trends and alerting over long periods → metrics (including log-based metrics). Exact messages and exceptions → log search. Which endpoint or dependency is slow or failing, with p95 by any facet → APM Trace Explorer. Start with metrics to scope, then drill into logs and traces. |

| :---- |

| 1 | Build Metric Queries and a p95 Latency Query*Datadog Query Language SOP — Day 3 — Lab 4* | ⏱ 7 min |
| :---: | :---- | :---: |

Metric queries combine an aggregator, a metric, a tag scope, a group-by and functions. You graph request rate by resource, build an error-ratio formula for the backend, use percentiles on the duration distribution and compare p95 with the average — first healthy, then with the CreditCardCheckError500 fault.

| ⌨  Task 1 — Metrics Explorer / a Notebook (one graph per query) |
| :---- |
|  |
| \# Q1 — request rate per resource of the backend |
| sum:trace.servlet.request.hits{env:cohort,service:easytravel-backend} by {resource\_name}.as\_rate()  ![][image4] |
|  |
| \# Q2 — backend error ratio (graph with two queries and a formula) |
| \#   a: sum:trace.servlet.request.errors{env:cohort,service:easytravel-backend}.as\_count() ![][image5]  |
| \#   b: sum:trace.servlet.request.hits{env:cohort,service:easytravel-backend}.as\_count() |
| \#   formula: 100 \* a / b |
| ![][image6] |
| \# Q3 — p95 latency: Metrics → Summary → trace.servlet.request → check it is a distribution, then graph: ![][image7] |
| P95:trace.servlet.request{env:cohort,service:easytravel-backend} ![][image8] |
| avg:trace.servlet.request{env:cohort,service:easytravel-backend} |
| ![][image9]  |
| \# CUE C1: when the instructor announces "CreditCardCheckError500 ON", write the time down, wait 3 minutes, look at Q2 and Q3 again |
| **📟  Expected Output** |
| Q1: one line per resource; the page and search resources have the highest rates, the booking resource a lower one (exact values depend on the load generator) |
| Q2: close to 0 % before the fault, clearly above 0 % during CreditCardCheckError500 (the shared Error Rate monitor from Day 2 uses 5 %) |
| Q3: p95 changes less than the error ratio, because failed requests return quickly; the all-requests average hides both — use the error ratio together with p95 |
| **1.A  Explain each part of Q1: space aggregator, metric, tag scope, group-by, function.**  Answer:  Space aggregator (`sum`): Adds the metric values across matching series. Metric: trace.servlet.request.hits counts the requests handled by the backend. Tag scope: {env:cohort,service:easytravel-backend} keeps only the easyTravel backend in this environment. Group-by: {resource\_name} separates results by request resource. Function (as\_rate()): Converts the count into requests per second. |
| **1.B  Why does Q3 use a percentile, and why is the all-requests average a poor signal here?**  Answer: Percentiles come from the distribution metric and show the slow tail that an average hides. The average mixes fast and slow requests, and during CreditCardCheckError500 it hides the failing requests completely, so p95 plus the error ratio is a better signal than the average.  |

| :---- |

| 4 | Create a Log-Based Metric and Query It*Datadog Query Language SOP — Day 3 — Lab 4* | ⏱ 7 min |
| :---: | :---- | :---: |

A log-based metric counts matching logs as they are ingested and stores the result as a metric with selected tags. You create one for easyTravel errors by service, watch new errors appear when the instructor switches the CreditCardCheckError500 fault on again, and query the metric like any other.

| ⌨  Task 4 — Generate Metrics |
| ----- |
|  |
| \# Step 1 (UI): Logs → Generate Metrics → New Metric |
| \#   Query: env:cohort status:error   ·   Measure: Count   ·   Group by: service   ·   Name: obslab.u\<seat\>.log.errors → Create |
| ![][image19] ![][image20] |
| \# Step 2: CUE C3 — once your metric exists, the instructor announces "CreditCardCheckError500 ON"; write the time down (metrics count only logs ingested after creation) |
|  |
| \# Step 3 (after 3 minutes): Metrics Explorer |
| sum:obslab.u\<seat\>.log.errors{\*} by {service}.as\_count() ![][image21] |
| sum:obslab.u\<seat\>.log.errors{\*}.as\_count().rollup(sum, 300\) ![][image22] |
|  |
| \# Step 4: end of the lab — CUE C4: the instructor announces "fault OFF"; write the time down |
| **📟  Expected Output** |
| Step 3: series for the easyTravel services, rising from the fault start time; nothing before the metric existed |
|         rollup(sum, 300): errors per 5 minutes (one bar per 5-minute interval) |
| **4.A  Why are there no data points before you created the metric, although the logs exist?**  Answer: Log-based metrics count only logs ingested after the metric is created. Older logs are not processed retroactively. |
| **4.B  Give two reasons to monitor obslab.u\<seat\>.log.errors instead of a logs query, and one tag you must never group a log-based metric by.**  Answer: Metrics are more efficient for long-term trend monitoring and alerting. They also use less storage and are easier to aggregate. Never group by high-cardinality tags such as `trace_id`. |

# 6\. TROUBLESHOOTING — COMMON ISSUES & FIXES

| Issue / Error | Cause | Diagnosis | Fix |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Metric not found | Agent or tracer not reporting, or the name differs | Metrics → Summary search "trace.servlet" | Tell your instructor; use the exact name shown in Metrics → Summary |
| p95 option missing | Metric is not a distribution, or the wrong metric name | Metrics Summary → metric → Advanced | Use trace.servlet.request (the distribution) shown in Metrics → Summary; tell your instructor if it is missing |
| Tag filter returns nothing | Tag key/value differs (e.g. service vs service.name) | Open the metric in Summary → Tags | Use the tags listed there |
| @logger.name search returns nothing | Attribute name differs or no facet | Open a log → attributes | Check that the @logger.name facet exists in the Log Explorer facet list; tell your instructor if it is missing — do not create duplicates |
| Trace Explorer empty | Live search window or env filter | Remove filters; check APM → Services | Use Live Search (15 min) and env:cohort |
| obslab.u\<seat\>.log.errors has no data | No new error logs since creation | Check the instructor's last cue; Log Explorer for new errors | Create the metric before the second fault cue; ask the instructor to repeat the cue if you were late |

# 7\. INSTRUCTOR DEBRIEF — 7 MINUTES

## 7.1  Discussion Questions

| Discussion 1 — Anatomy of a Metric Query |
| :---- |
| Without notes: write the backend p95 query and the error-ratio formula. |
| Which part changes when you move the query into a monitor? |
|  |
| Key answer to explore: same query plus a time aggregation window and threshold, e.g. avg(last\_5m):… \> 1\. |
| **Discussion 2 — Tags vs Attributes** |
| Which questions could you answer only in logs/traces, not in metrics? |
| Why must high-cardinality values stay attributes? |
|  |
| Key insight: metrics group by tags only; attributes with facets serve detailed analysis without cardinality cost. |
| **Discussion 3 — APM Facets** |
| How did the status and @http.status\_code facets change the investigation compared with service names alone? |
| Which facets would you add to the standard Trace Explorer view? |
|  |
| Key answer: they name the failing request and its error; add resource\_name, @http.status\_code, version. |
| **Discussion 4 — Log-to-Metric Economics** |
| When would you keep the logs and when only the metric? |
| What does the 20-minute ingestion rule mean for back-filling? |
|  |
| Answer: keep logs for investigation windows, metrics for long trends and monitors; log-based metrics cannot be back-filled. |

## 7.2  Common Mistakes — Learn From These

| Mistake | Why It Happens | Consequence | Prevention |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| avg for latency | Default aggregator | Slow tail invisible | p95/p99 on distributions or APM |
| Unscoped queries | {\*} everywhere | Mixed services and resources | Scope by service, resource, env |
| @ on tags / no @ on attributes | Similar syntax | Empty results | Tags without @, attributes with @ |
| as\_count vs as\_rate confusion | Both look plausible | Wrong numbers in graphs/monitors | as\_count for totals per interval, as\_rate per second |
| Log-based metric expected to back-fill | Assumption | Empty graphs | Create first, then generate events |

# 10\. QUICK REFERENCE — DATADOG QUERY LANGUAGE COMMAND CARD

Bookmark this page. Every command you need in SOP order.

| Category | Command | Purpose |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Metric | sum:metric{tag:value} by {tag}.as\_rate() | Anatomy |
| Wildcard tag | {status:5\*} | Tag value prefix |
| Formula | a: errors.as\_count() · b: hits.as\_count() · 100 \* a / b | Error ratio |
| Percentile | p95:distribution\_metric{…} | Distribution metric |
| Rollup | .rollup(sum, 300\) | Time aggregation |
| Log tag | service:easytravel-backend status:error | No @ |
| Log attribute | @logger.name:"\<value\>" | Facet |
| Phrase / exclude | "CreditCardCheckError500" \-service:easytravel-frontend | Search |
| Trace facets | service · resource\_name · status · @http.status\_code | APM |
| APM p95 | Visualize → p95 of Duration by resource\_name | Latency |
| Log-based metric | Logs → Generate Metrics → query, measure, group by | Counts new logs |
| Use in monitor | avg(last\_5m):\<metric query\> \> threshold | Lab 5 |

# APPENDIX A — INSTRUCTOR PRE-CLASS RUNBOOK (INSTRUCTOR ONLY)

INSTRUCTOR ONLY — learners never run these commands. easyTravel runs on the EC2 host ip-172-30-0-220 (SSH as the instructor) with Datadog Agent 7 and dd-java-agent.jar, the same setup as Day 2 Labs 8–9.  
1\. At least 30 minutes before class confirm in Datadog: Infrastructure shows the host; APM → Services lists easytravel-frontend and easytravel-backend with env:cohort; Metrics → Summary shows trace.servlet.request, trace.servlet.request.hits and trace.servlet.request.errors; Logs → Search env:cohort returns easyTravel logs. Confirm the fault is off.  
2\. In Datadog (admin): create the @logger.name facet once (open an error log → attribute logger.name → Create facet) so learners do not create duplicates. Give learners the standard role; they create only their own log-based metric obslab.u01.log.errors … obslab.u40.log.errors — confirm the trial limit on custom log-based metrics is not exceeded for 40 seats.  
3\. Fault cues (announce each time and write it on the board): C0 start of Task 1: fault off. C1 about 3 minutes into Task 1: fault ON. C2 about T+16, before Task 3 ends: announce "fault OFF" while learners create their log-based metric. C3 once most learners have the metric (about T+23): fault ON again. C4 about T+28: fault OFF. Commands on the EC2 host:

| ⌨  Instructor — Fault ON / OFF (run on ip-172-30-0-220) |
| :---- |
|  |
| \# Fault ON (C1, C3) |
| curl \-s "http\://localhost:8091/services/ConfigurationService/setPluginEnabled?name=CreditCardCheckError500\&enabled=true"; date \+%T |
| \# Fault OFF (C2, C4) |
| curl \-s "http\://localhost:8091/services/ConfigurationService/setPluginEnabled?name=CreditCardCheckError500\&enabled=false"; date \+%T |

4\. After the fault turns on, allow 2–3 minutes for the Datadog monitors, traces and logs to show it. At the end of the lab confirm the fault is off.
